<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:exist-reg}
Let $\mathcal{O}$ be a bounded convex domain in ${\mathbb R}^{n}$ with smooth boundary $\partial\mathcal{O}$, and let $p,q$ be two points in ${\mathbb R}^n\setminus\overline\mathcal{O}$. Then there exists a minimizer of \eqref{eq:E} in the admissible set $\mathcal{A}$, and any minimizer is a $C^1$ curve with bounded curvature depending only on the maximum principal curvature of $\partial\mathcal{O}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:unique}
Fix a point $p$ in ${\mathbb R}^n\setminus \overline\mathcal{O}$. 
Let $\mathcal{S}_1$ and $\mathcal{S}_{2}$ denote the sets of points $q$ in ${\mathbb R}^n\setminus \overline \mathcal{O}$ for which the minimizer of the energy \eqref{eq:E} over $\mathcal{A}$ is unique and non-unique, respectively. Then $\mathcal{S}_2 \subset \partial \mathcal{S}_1$, and in particular $\operatorname{int}(\mathcal{S}_2)=\emptyset$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:vision}
Let $\mathcal{O}$ be a bounded convex domain in ${\mathbb R}^n$. 
A cone with apex $p$ is called the \textit{vision cone} of $p$ (relative to $\mathcal{O}$) if it is tangent to $\mathcal{O}$. The intersection of the vision cone and $\partial\mathcal{O}$ is called the \textit{vision boundary} of $p$. The vision cone and vision boundary will be denoted by $\mathcal{C}_p$ and $\Gamma_p$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:charac}
Any minimizer of \eqref{eq:E} over $\mathcal{A}$ consists of a geodesic on $\partial\mathcal{O}$ that connects two vision boundary $\Gamma_p$ and $\Gamma_q$, with two line segments connecting the points $p$ and $q$ to the vision boundaries $\Gamma_p$ and $\Gamma_q$, respectively.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- thmx-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:reg}
Let $u\in \mathcal{A}$ be a energy minimizer of \eqref{eq:E} over $\mathcal{A}$. Then $u\in C^{1,1}_{loc}(I)$.
<!-- end thmx-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:exist}
There exists a solution $\mathbf{u}:[0,1]\rightarrow \mathcal{O}^c$ minimizing energy \eqref{eq:E} over the admissible set $\mathcal{A}$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal{O}$ is bounded, any two points outside $\mathcal{O}$ are connected by a smooth curve in $\mathcal{O}^c$, which induces that $\mathcal{A}$ is not empty. We now take a minimizing sequence $\mathbf{u}_k \in \mathcal{A}$ such that 
\begin{align}
\lim_{k\rightarrow \infty} E(\mathbf{u}_k) = \inf_{\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{A}} E(\mathbf{v}).
\end{align}

Let $c:I\rightarrow \mathcal{O}^c$ be a smooth curve connecting two points $p$ and $q$. Since $c\in \mathcal{A}$, we have $\inf_{\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{A}}E(\mathbf{v})\le E(c)<\infty$, and thus $E(\mathbf{u}_k)$ is uniformly bounded. Using the Poincar\`e inequality, $\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_k\right\rVert_{H^1}$ is also uniformly bounded. Then there exists a function $\mathbf{u}\in H^1(I;{\mathbb R}^n)$ such that a subsequence of $\mathbf{u}_k$ converges weakly to $\mathbf{u}$ in $H^1(I;{\mathbb R}^n)$ and converges (strongly) to $\mathbf{u}$ almost everywhere in $I$. We still denote by $\mathbf{u}_k$ the converging subsequence. 

Clearly, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathcal{A}$ since $\mathbf{u}_k(0)=p$, $\mathbf{u}_k(1)=q$, and $\mathbf{u}_k(I)$ is contained in the closed set $\mathcal{O}^c$. Moreover, since $E$ is weakly lower semicontinuous on $H^1(I;{\mathbb R}^n)$, we have
\begin{align}
E(\mathbf{u})\le\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty} E(\mathbf{u}_k)=\inf_{\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{A}}E(\mathbf{v})\le E(\mathbf{u})
\end{align}
which conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ is a minimizer of $E$ on $\mathcal{A}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The result follows from \Cref{thm:reg}, \Cref{lem:exist}, and the fact that $\mathbf{u}''=0$ holds away from the obstacle, as stated in \eqref{eq:EL}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:La}
The coincidence set $\Lambda$ is of the form $[a,b]$ for some $a,b \in (0,1)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since the non-coincidence set $\Omega=\{t\in[0,1]: \mathbf{u}(t)\in {\mathbb R}^n\setminus \overline{\mathcal{O}}\}$ is open in $[0,1]$ and $\{0,1\}\subset \Omega$, the non-coincidence set $\Omega$ is of the form 
\begin{align}
\Omega=[0,a)\cup \bigcup_{k=1}^m(a_k,b_k)\cup(b,1]
\end{align}
for some $m\in \mathbb{N}\cup \{0,\infty\}$. We claim that $m=0$. If $m>0$, then for each $(a_k,b_k)$, it holds
\begin{align}
\mathbf{u}(t)\notin \mathcal{O} \text{ for } t\in (a_k,b_k) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{u}(a_k),\mathbf{u}(b_k)\in \partial\mathcal{O}.
\end{align}

Let $\mathbf{v}:[a_k,b_k]\rightarrow \partial \mathcal{O}$ be the projected curve of $\mathbf{u}\vert_{[a_k,b_k]}$ into $\partial\mathcal{O}$. Then, we can express $\mathbf{u}$ as $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{v}+hN$, where $N$ is the outward unit normal to $\partial\mathcal{O}$ and $h:[0,1] \rightarrow {\mathbb R}$ is a nonnegative function satisfying $h(a_k)=h(b_k)=0$ and $h(t)>0$ for $a_k<t<b_k$ so that
\begin{align}
\int_{a_k}^{b_k} |h'|^2>0.
\end{align}
Hence, noting $\mathbf{v}'\cdot N=0$ and $N'\cdot N=0$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Eu-Ev}
\begin{split}
\int_{a_k}^{b_k}|\mathbf{u}'(t)|^2-|\mathbf{v}'(t)|^2&=2\int_{a_k}^{b_k} \mathbf{v}'\cdot (hN)' +\int_{a_k}^{b_k} |(hN)'|^2
\\
&=
2\int_{a_k}^{b_k} (\mathbf{v}'\cdot N')h+\int_{a_k}^{b_k} |h'|^2 + h^2|N'|^2 >0
\end{split}
\end{equation}
since $\mathbf{v}'\cdot N'=-\mathbf{v}''\cdot N \ge 0$ by the convexity of the obstacle $\mathcal{O}$ and $h> 0$ in $(a_k,b_k)$. 

Let $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}$ be the function derived from $\mathbf{u}$ by replacing $\mathbf{u}$ with $\mathbf{v}$ over the interval $(a_k,b_k)$. Then it follows from \eqref{eq:Eu-Ev} that $E(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}) < E(\mathbf{u})$. This contradicts the assumption that $\mathbf{u}$ minimizes energy. Therefore, we must have $m=0$, which implies that $\Omega = [0, a) \cup (b,1]$ and $\Lambda=[a,b]$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:u-Ga}
Let $\Gamma_p$ be the vision boundary of $p$ with respect to $\mathcal{O}$ (\Cref{def:vision}). Then $\mathbf{u}(a) \in \Gamma_p$ and $\mathbf{u}([0,a])$ is the line segment connecting $p$ and $\mathbf{u}(a)$. Similarly, $\mathbf{u}(b) \in \Gamma_q$ and $\mathbf{u}([b,1])$ is the line segment connecting $\mathbf{u}(b)$ and $q$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
On the non-coincidence set $[0,a)$, it follows from the Euler--Lagrange equation that $\mathbf{u}''=0$. Thus $\mathbf{u}([0,a])$ is the line segment connecting $p$ and $\mathbf{u}(a)$.

To prove $\mathbf{u}(a)\in \Gamma_p$, we note that $\Gamma_p$ divides $\partial\mathcal{O}$ into two parts. Let us denote the piece that is closer to the point $p$ as $\partial\mathcal{O}_p$.
If $\mathbf{u}(a)\not\in \Gamma_p$, then $\mathbf{u}(a)\in \partial\mathcal{O}_p$.
Since $l_{pq}\cap \mathcal{O}\not=\emptyset$, we see that $\mathbf{u}(b)$ lies in the other piece of $\partial\mathcal{O}$. Thus there exists $t_0\in (a,b)$ such that $\mathbf{u}(t_0)\in \Gamma_p$. However, replacing $\mathbf{u}([0,t_0])$ with the line segment connecting $p$ and $\mathbf{u}(t_0)$ reduces energy, which is a contradiction. Therefore, $\mathbf{u}(a)\in \Gamma_p$. 

The same argument shows the similar statement for $q$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
The coincidence set $\Lambda$ is not a single point, i.e., $a<b$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Suppose $a=b$. Given the smoothness of $\partial \mathcal{O}$, $\mathbf{u}(a)$ has a unique tangent plane of $\partial\mathcal{O}$ at $\mathbf{u}(a)$. By virtue of \Cref{lem:u-Ga}, both points $p$ and $q$ are situated on this tangent plane. This, however, leads to a contradiction, as it implies that the line segment $l_{pq}$ has no intersection with $\mathcal{O}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:geo}
The restriction $\mathbf{u}\vert_{[a,b]}$ is a minimizing geodesic joining $\mathbf{u}(a)$ and $\mathbf{u}(b)$ on $\partial\mathcal{O}$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $f:[a,b]\rightarrow{\mathbb R}$ be a function with $f(t)>0$ in $(a,b)$ and $f(a)=f(b)=0$, and let $V(t)=f(t) \nabla_{\mathbf{u}'}\mathbf{u}'$.
Consider a variation $F:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times [a,b]\rightarrow \partial\mathcal{O}$ of $\mathbf{u}\vert_{[a,b]}$ having $V(t)$ as variational field, i.e., $F(0,t)=\mathbf{u}\vert_{[a,b]}$, $F(\cdot,a)\equiv\mathbf{u}(a)$, $F(\cdot,b)\equiv\mathbf{u}(b)$, and $\frac{\partial F}{\partial s}(0,\cdot)=V$.

Let $E(s)$ be the energy of the perturbed curve $F(s,\cdot)$. By differentiating 
\begin{align}
E(s) = \int_a^b |\partial_tF(s,t)|^2 dt
\end{align}
with respect to $s$, we have
\begin{align}
\partial_s \int_a^b |\partial_tF(s,t)|^2 dt = 2\int_a^b \left\langle {\nabla_{s}\partial_t F},{\partial_t F} \right\rangle dt=2\int_a^b \left\langle {\nabla_{t}\partial_s F},{\partial_t F} \right\rangle dt.
\end{align}
Using the integration by parts, we obtain
\begin{align}
\int_a^b \left\langle {\nabla_{t}\partial_s F},{\partial_t F} \right\rangle dt
&=
\int_a^b \partial_t\left\langle {\partial_s F},{\partial_t F} \right\rangle dt - \int_a^b \left\langle {\partial_s F},{\nabla_{t}\partial_t F} \right\rangle dt
\\
&=\left\langle {\partial_s F},{\partial_t F} \right\rangle\vert_a^b - \int_a^b \left\langle {\partial_s F},{\nabla_{t}\partial_t F} \right\rangle dt.
\end{align}
Taking $s=0$, we conclude that
\begin{align}
0=\tfrac{1}{2}E'(0)&= \left\langle {V(b)},{\mathbf{u}(b)} \right\rangle-\left\langle {V(a)},{\mathbf{u}(a)} \right\rangle- \int_a^b \left\langle {V(t)},{\nabla_{\mathbf{u}'}\mathbf{u}'} \right\rangle dt
\\
&=-\int_a^b f(t)|\nabla_{\mathbf{u}'}\mathbf{u}'|^2dt.
\end{align}
Therefore, we have $\nabla_{\mathbf{u}'}\mathbf{u}'=0$ in $(a,b)$, meaning that $\mathbf{u}$ is indeed a geodesic.

The fact that this geodesic is minimizing follows from the equality condition given in \eqref{ineq:LE}. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The proof follows from \Cref{lem:La}-\Cref{lem:geo}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:unique}
Fix a point $p$ in $\mathcal{O}^c$. Assume that $\mathbf{u}\in \mathcal{A}$ is a minimizer of \eqref{eq:E}. Then the energy-minimizing curve in $\mathcal{A}$ with respect to $p$ and $q'$, where $q'$ is an intermediate point between $\mathbf{u}(b)$ and $q$, is unique.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Consider the vision boundaries $\Gamma_q$ and $\Gamma_{q'}$. Note that $\Gamma_q$ partitions $\partial\mathcal{O}$ into two distinct regions, with $\Gamma_{q'}\setminus \mathbf{u}(b)$ contained in one of these regions. Furthermore, observe that $\mathbf{u}(b)$ lies in the intersection of $\Gamma_q$ and $\Gamma_{q'}$.



We begin by noting that
\begin{align}\label{eq:diff-min}
|q'-\mathbf{u}(b)|-|q-\mathbf{u}(b)|=-|q'-q|.
\end{align}
Select a point $x'$ in $\Gamma_{q'}$, distinct from $\mathbf{u}(b)$, and let $x$ denote the intersection of $\Gamma_q$ and the geodesic starting at $x'$, directed towards $x'-q'$. Define $l$ as the length of the minimizing geodesic that connects $x'$ and $x$. By the triangle inequality in the triangle $xqq'$, we find
\begin{align}\label{eq:diff-any}
(|q'-x'|+l)-|q-x|>|q'-x|-|q-x|>-|q'-q|.
\end{align}

By comparing \eqref{eq:diff-min} with \eqref{eq:diff-any}, and using \Cref{thm:charac}, we deduce the uniqueness of the energy minimizer for the given fixed points $p$ and $q'$, thereby concluding the proof.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For any point $q$ in $\mathcal{S}_2$, \Cref{lem:unique} implies the existence of a line segment contained in $\mathcal{S}_1$. Therefore, $q\in \partial \mathcal{S}_1$. The assertion $\operatorname{int}\mathcal{S}_2=\emptyset$ naturally follows from $\mathcal{S}_2\subseteq \partial \mathcal{S}_1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj}
Fix a point $p$ in ${\mathbb R}^n\setminus \overline\mathcal{O}$. 
Let $\mathcal{S}_{2}$ denotes the set of points $q$ in ${\mathbb R}^n\setminus \overline \mathcal{O}$ for which the minimizer of the energy \eqref{eq:E} over $\mathcal{A}$ is not unique. Then the Hausdorff dimension of $\mathcal{S}_2$ is at most $n-1$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
